formula: guessed total trip length through node n
example: Values of three actions: 4, 9, 7. max = 9 (a value); argmax = action 2 (which one).
cards.memory: max answers HOW GOOD, argmax answers WHICH ONE.
cards.trap: Policies use argmax; utilities use max. Writing the value when the action is asked loses the mark.
explain: Maths is a language: each symbol is a short way to write a phrase. f(n) = g(n) + h(n) reads 'f of n equals g of n plus h of n', meaning the distance already travelled plus a guess of the distance still to go.
A hat means 'estimate' (ŷ), a bar means 'average' (ȳ). A small lowered number is a label (x₂ = the second x); a raised number is a power (x² = x × x).
Calculator skills for the exam: ln, log, eˣ, xʸ and √. Check yourself: log₂8 = 3, ln 2 = 0.693, e⁻¹ = 0.368, 0.8³⁰ = 0.00124, 1/(1 + e^−0.6) = 0.646.

cards.title: Functions, lines, curves and optima
cards.hook: A model, a loss, a heuristic and a policy are all functions: input in, one output out.
cards.visual:
FunctionInput → output

loss Lweights → how wrong
heuristic h(n)node → guessed distance

ReLUz → max(0, z)
formula: y = w₁x + w₀ (slope w₁, intercept w₀)
example: y = x² − 4x + 7 = (x − 2)² + 3: minimum at x = 2, y = 3 (Lecture 3's continuous problem).
Lecture 4's data y = 4x + 5: at x = −4, y = −11.
cards.memory: Minimise f = maximise −f (that is why hill climbing maximises −cost).
cards.trap: A local minimum is lowest only among its neighbours; hill climbing can stop there.
explain: A function takes an input and gives exactly one output, like a vending machine.
A straight line y = w₁x + w₀ has slope w₁ (rise per unit of x) and intercept w₀ (value at x = 0). Linear regression learns these two numbers.
A U-shaped quadratic ax² + bx + c (a > 0) has its lowest point at x = −b/(2a). Completing the square shows why: x² − 4x + 7 = (x − 2)² + 3, and a square is never negative.
Piecewise functions use different rules on different inputs: ReLU(z) = z if z > 0 else 0; the perceptron step is 1 if z ≥ 0 else 0.

cards.title: Powers, e and logarithms
cards.hook: Logs appear in entropy, cross-entropy and Naive Bayes; exponentials in sigmoid, softmax, SA and discounting.
formula: log(ab) = log a + log b; log(aⁿ) = n log a
example: 0.8³⁰ = (0.8¹⁰)³ = 0.107³ ≈ 0.0012: the vanishing gradient in the Lecture 8 poll.
cards.memory: Entropy has a minus sign because every log₂p is negative for p < 1.
cards.trap: Entropy uses log₂; cross-entropy, KL and GAN loss use ln. Using log₁₀ is the classic slip.
explain: aⁿ means a multiplied by itself n times. The full joint table has 2ⁿ rows; BFS visits about bᵈ nodes; discount weights are γᵏ.
e ≈ 2.718. eˣ is always positive, equals 1 at x = 0, grows fast for positive x and shrinks to 0 for negative x. That is why sigmoid is 0.5 at z = 0 and softmax makes every score positive.
A logarithm undoes a power: log₂8 = 3 because 2³ = 8. Logs of numbers between 0 and 1 are negative, log 1 = 0, and in entropy 0 log 0 = 0.
Logs turn products into sums: Naive Bayes can add log-probabilities instead of multiplying tiny numbers, and the winning class stays the same.

cards.title: Σ, Π and weighted averages
cards.hook: Σ adds a list, Π multiplies it. A weighted average is behind expected utility, weighted entropy and attention.

cards.memory: Σ = Sum, Π = Product (P for Product).
cards.trap: Weighted child entropy uses the branch SHARES |Sₖ|/|S| as weights, not a plain average.
explain: The counter i under Σ says where to start, the number on top where to stop. A double sum ΣᵢΣⱼ runs over every pair, like every cell of a convolution kernel.
A weighted average multiplies each value by a weight and adds. When the weights are probabilities it is an expected value.

cards.title: Vectors, dot products and matrices
cards.hook: Data points, images and word embeddings are vectors. Attention scores and neurons are dot products.
example: Embedding lookup: one-hot (0,0,1,0,0,0) × E = row 2 of E.
cards.memory: Big dot product = same direction; zero = unrelated; negative = opposite.
cards.trap: (m × n)(n × p) = m × p: inner sizes must match.
explain: A vector is an ordered list of numbers. Add or scale entry by entry.
The dot product multiplies matching entries and adds; the result is one number measuring alignment. Attention uses q·k to score relevance.
A matrix times a vector gives one dot product per row. Matrix × matrix needs the inner sizes to match.
A tensor is the general shape: a PyTorch image batch is [batch, channels, height, width]. Printing shapes is the best debugging habit.

cards.title: Derivatives, chain rule, gradient descent
cards.hook: Every learning algorithm: measure the error, find which way reduces it (the derivative), take a small step.

example: y = x² − 4x + 7: y′ = 2x − 4; at x = 4 slope 4; at x = 2 slope 0 (minimum).
Neuron loss L = (y − h)², h = σ(z): ∂L/∂w₁ = −2(y − h)h(1 − h)x₁.
cards.memory: Gears: effects along a chain MULTIPLY. Many factors below 1 → vanishing gradient.
cards.trap: Too large α overshoots and can diverge; too small is slow.
explain: The derivative f′(x) is the slope of the tangent at x: positive = uphill to the right, zero = possible minimum or maximum.
Chain rule: if y depends on u and u on x, multiply the two slopes. Backpropagation applies it layer by layer.
The sigmoid's slope peaks at 0.25 (at z = 0). Ten sigmoid layers give at most 0.25¹⁰ ≈ 10⁻⁶: vanishing gradients.
With several inputs, a partial derivative holds the others fixed. The gradient (all partials) points uphill, so gradient descent steps against it.

tex.t: \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1}=\underbrace{-2(y-h)}_{\partial L/\partial h}\cdot\underbrace{h(1-h)}_{\partial h/\partial z}\cdot\underbrace{x_1}_{\partial z/\partial w_1}

cards.title: Probability from scratch
cards.hook: Probability is the maths of uncertainty: MDPs, Naive Bayes, generative models and Bayesian networks all rest on it.

example: Medical test (prior 1%, sensitivity 90%, false positive 5%): P(+) = 0.0585; P(sick|+) = 0.154.
cards.memory: GIVEN = shrink the world to where B happened, then ask how often A happens.
cards.trap: Add only for mutually exclusive events; otherwise subtract the overlap.
explain: With equally likely outcomes, P(A) = favourable/total. A random variable is a quantity whose value is uncertain (Burglary: true/false).
Independence: knowing B tells you nothing about A, P(A|B) = P(A). Conditional independence: once C is known, B adds nothing.
Marginalising ('summing out') a joint table gives the probability of one variable; dividing gives conditionals.
Bayes' rule flips a conditional. The normalising α just makes the answers add to 1, which is why Naive Bayes can compare scores directly.
Gaussians N(μ, σ²) appear in VAEs (the N(0, I) prior) and diffusion (added noise). Probabilities are usually estimated by counting: ADP, n-grams and Naive Bayes all do this.
